studies.title: The chromatophore as an actuator: mechanics, kinetics and a datasheet
studies.question: A cephalopod chromatophore is a pigment sac opened by radial muscle under direct motor-neuron control. Treat it as an actuator and write its datasheet: what stroke, what speed, what force, what does it cost to hold open - and does a physical model of it reproduce what was measured?
studies.summary: Two parameters are fitted to two measured quantities and the two fits are mutually inconsistent. The sacculus shear modulus is fitted to the 2.5506x steady-state expansion ratio; the dermal damping is then fitted to the measured expansion:retraction asymmetry and reaches it (1.27 against 1.34 from Renard 2026, while Hadjisolomou 2021 decomposed per region gives 3.7) - but at that damping the peak expansion collapses to 1.73, 32% short of the ratio the stiffness was fitted to. **The one genuinely free prediction fails**: the 90% rise is 232 ms against a measured expansion phase of 67-83 ms, 2.8-3.5x too slow. An earlier version of this study claimed a lumped elastic recoil was STRUCTURALLY incapable of retraction slower than expansion; that was wrong - it was read off a sweep whose maximum sat at its own boundary - and the correction is recorded in the file rather than edited out. The parameter ledger is the study's own indictment: 5 sourced against 13 assumed, with every muscle property an explicit proxy from a different Doryteuthis muscle because nobody has measured a chromatophore radial muscle. Its most useful output is negative: across every sweep the stroke is set by the elastic sac rather than by the muscle, so adding radial fibres buys almost nothing.

figures.alt: A two-part figure. On the left, a 22-row datasheet table for one chromatophore organ, listing addressable unit, retracted and expanded pigment disc area, area expansion ratio, linear stroke, fibre shortening, blocked and holding force, holding stress, isometric duty, stored elastic energy, work density, rise and retraction times, response latency, bandwidth, in-vivo flicker rate, independent control inputs, array density, power supply and return mechanism; six rows are highlighted in green as measured rather than modelled. Top right, a simulated step response: the pigment area ratio rises to about 2.06 during a 250 ms drive window and relaxes back to 1.0 by about 400 ms, with a dashed line at the measured 2.55 that the curve never reaches. Bottom right, a log-scale comparison of three quantities, each showing the model value as a coloured dot and the measured value or range as a grey bar: area ratio model 2.06 against measured 2.55, rise time model 215 ms against measured 117-150 ms, and retraction-over-expansion model 0.49 against measured 1.34.
figures.caption: Simulation, not a measurement. The datasheet is model output except for the six rows marked MEASURED. The bottom-right panel is the control arm and it fails: only the area ratio was fitted, and the one free prediction - the rise time - falls outside the measured range, while the expansion-to-retraction asymmetry comes out on the wrong side of 1.

figures.alt: Six panels of parameter sweeps. Top row: steady-state area expansion ratio against the number of radial muscle fibres, rising steeply to about 20 fibres and then flat at the measured 2.55; against sacculus shear modulus, flat at 2.55 below about 80 kPa and falling steeply above it, with the fitted modulus marked; and against maximum fibre shortening, rising linearly to 30 per cent and flat thereafter, with the stroke-limited region shaded. Bottom row: expansion and retraction times against radial fibre length, with expansion flat near 215 ms above the measured 117-150 ms band and retraction falling from 155 to 80 ms; expansion and retraction times against dermal damping, both nearly flat across nine orders of magnitude; and a heat map of area ratio over fibre number and sacculus modulus, with the muscle-stroke-limited region hatched and the measured 2.55 contour drawn.
figures.caption: Simulation, not a measurement. Each panel varies one parameter about the baseline. The shape that matters is in the first and third panels: the organ sits on the flat part of the fibre-number curve and on the flat part of the shortening curve, so it is limited by the elasticity of the pigment sac and not by its muscle. Dermal damping is the only knob that touches retraction, and it has never been measured.

studies.title: A pigment layer over a tunable Bragg reflector: how much colour is reachable, and which layer stops it
studies.kind: optical model (transfer-matrix multilayer + areal pigment mixing + CIE colorimetry)
studies.question: Cephalopod skin stacks a pigment actuator over a tunable multilayer reflector over a broadband scatterer. Given the measured optical parameters of each, what colours can that stack actually reach under a stated illuminant - and which layer is the one holding it back?
studies.summary: Freezing the iridophore stack removes 89% of the achievable chromaticity area, so the multilayer is what produces the colour - but the layer that PROVIDES the gamut is not the layer that LIMITS it. Widening the stack's measured 425-675 nm tuning range to the whole visible band buys 1%, while raising the reflectin refractive index from the live-cell mean 1.405 to the measured maximum 1.44 buys 68% and a nearly transparent retracted state buys 61%. **The study's weakness is entirely on the pigment side**: the Bragg stack's layer count, both refractive indices, both thicknesses and its tuning range are published numbers from live cells, but no measured absorption spectrum for any cephalopod ommochrome was found, so all nine pigment numbers are assumed and every hue in the gamut inherits that (9 sourced against 8 assumed). It is also a steady-state, normal-incidence model under CIE D65 and a HUMAN observer, which is wrong on three counts at once: real iridophores are strongly angle-dependent, seawater is not D65, and the animals that matter are a colour-blind cephalopod and a tetrachromatic fish. One of its four controls fails, and the failure is in the source rather than the model - the published endpoint thicknesses do not reproduce the published tuning range under the paper's own refractive indices.

figures.alt: Two panels. Left, a CIE 1976 u-prime v-prime chromaticity diagram with the horseshoe-shaped spectral locus outlined in grey and four overlapping shaded polygons showing achievable chromaticities: the largest is the hypothetical case with the reflectin refractive index at its measured maximum, inside it the achievable set with every dial free, and two much smaller regions for chromatophores held expanded and for the iridophore stack held fixed; the D65 white point is marked with a cross near the middle of the achievable set. Right, reflectance against wavelength from 380 to 780 nanometres: four narrow peaks of about 15 per cent reflectance for stacks tuned to 440, 520, 600 and 660 nanometres with their layer thicknesses labelled, plus two broad dark curves for the whole skin with all pigment expanded and with all pigment retracted, both rising steeply towards the red end.
figures.caption: Optical model, not a measurement. The multilayer is a transfer-matrix calculation using measured live-cell parameters; the pigment layer above it uses an assumed absorption spectrum, because none was found. Note how close together the achievable set and the white point are: at the measured refractive-index contrast of 1.048 a nine-pair stack reflects only about 15 per cent at its peak, so the skin is never very saturated.

figures.alt: Two bar charts of gamut area relative to the full model. Left, ten horizontal bars: five orange bars for holding one layer fixed, showing the iridophore held at its live-cell mean at 0.11, chromatophores held retracted at 0.59, chromatophores held expanded at 0.26, the leucophore backing removed at 1.00 and the stack fixed at eight pairs at 0.87; and five green bars for widening one dial, showing chromatophore area ratio ten times at 1.48, Bragg tuning over the whole visible band at 1.01, reflectin index at its measured maximum at 1.68, area ratio fifty times at 1.61 and both optical dials at 1.76. Right, three yellow bars for removing one pigment class: without yellow the gamut is larger than the full model, without red it is about 0.73, and without brown it is essentially unchanged.
figures.caption: Optical model, not a measurement. Two questions with two different answers: freezing the iridophore costs 88 per cent of the gamut, so the stack is what provides the colour, but widening its tuning range buys one per cent while raising the refractive index buys sixty-eight, so index contrast is what limits it. Removing the yellow pigment class makes the gamut bigger, because at the only sourced expansion ratio a retracted chromatophore still covers 52 per cent of the skin and that floor is a pure loss.

studies.title: How many independent control channels does an addressable skin need?
studies.kind: simulation (pigment-actuator array + observer blur + projected-gradient controller)
studies.question: An array of pigment actuators at a measured spatial density is driven by N independent channels, each owning a motor unit of m actuators. How well can the skin match a target pattern, and where is the point of diminishing returns? The knee is the spec sheet for anyone building this.
studies.summary: At the measured motor-unit size of nine actuators per channel the knee sits at 579 +/- 0 channels over a 3904-actuator patch - about 36 channels per square millimetre, or one channel per 6.7 actuators - but quote it as 'between 306 and 1094, nearest grid point 579', NOT as '579 +/- 0'. The standard deviation across the 30 runs is genuinely 0.0 and that is a GRID ARTEFACT: channel count is swept on a 14-point logarithmic grid, so a knee can only land on a grid point and all 30 landed on the same one. What the agreement shows is that the knee is stable to within one grid step. Across unit sizes the knee tracks the count needed simply to COVER the array within a factor of 1.00-5.41, so for everything but the finest target the channel budget is set by innervating the skin at all, not by the complexity of the pattern. The real animal is not a free parameter here: Renard et al. 2026 resolved 754 putative motor units driving 1829 chromatophores, which is 0.412 channels per actuator with units of about nine, so a cuttlefish sits at 1609 channels on this patch and is PAST the knee on every target. **Its biggest weakness is that the addressable element is wrong**: motor units here own whole actuators, whereas a real chromatophore is driven by about four independent sources acting on contiguous angular sectors, so these channel counts are a lower bound on what a cuttlefish has. The observer's acuity is assumed and is the parameter the knee most likely depends on, no predator acuity number having been sourced; the coverage law is biased by up to 16 per cent relative and that control is reported as FAILED, with a sensitivity arm showing the knee does not move. Two optimiser bugs were caught by declared controls before they could ship as results, and both are documented in the file with the numbers they produced. 4 parameters are sourced against 4 assumed.
studies.summary_table_title: Knee by motor-unit size and target
studies.grid_caveat: The s.d. across seeds and targets is 0.0, and that is a GRID ARTEFACT, not a precision claim. The channel count is swept on a 14-point logarithmic grid, so a knee can only ever land on a grid point; every seed and every non-trivial target happened to land on the same one. The real uncertainty is therefore bounded below by the grid spacing, which here is a factor of about 1.9 in either direction - the neighbouring grid points are 306 and 1094. Quote the knee as 'between 306 and 1094, nearest grid point 579', not as '579 +/- 0'. A finer grid would be needed to say more, and the agreement across 30 independent runs is evidence that the knee is stable to within one grid step, which is a weaker and true statement.
studies.verification_gap: DECLARED AND NOT REACHED - this is a gap in verification, not a clean result

figures.alt: Six panels, one per target pattern - edge, square, coarse stripes, fine stripes, one-over-f gravel and mottle - each plotting pattern match as variance explained against the number of independent control channels on a logarithmic axis. Each panel carries five curves, one per motor-unit size of one, three, nine, fourteen and thirty actuators, with shaded bands for plus or minus one standard deviation across five array seeds, and a dotted vertical line marking each curve's knee. A solid black vertical line, with a black dot on the nine-actuator curve, marks the channel count a real cuttlefish uses, derived from published motor-unit counts. Every curve is flat near zero at low channel counts, rises steeply over about one decade, and saturates.
figures.caption: Simulation, not a measurement. The dotted lines are the knee as declared before the sweep ran: the smallest channel count reaching 95 per cent of the score at one channel per actuator. Larger motor units push the knee to the left, because fewer channels are needed to cover the array - and that, rather than the pattern's spatial detail, is what sets the budget for five of the six targets. The black line is the measured operating point of a real animal - 754 motor units over 1829 chromatophores in Euprymna berryi and Sepia officinalis - placed on our own curve, which is the comparison this study exists to make. The two uniform targets are not plotted: their variance is zero, so the score is undefined and is reported as null rather than as a vacuous 1.0.

figures.alt: A grid of greyscale images in two rows. The leftmost column is the target pattern, a soft one-over-f noise texture. Each subsequent column shows the modelled skin driven by an increasing number of channels, from a handful to one per actuator, with the achieved match score printed beneath each panel. The top row uses compact wiring and the bottom row the oracle wiring that is allowed to choose its motor units after seeing the target. Panels at low channel counts are nearly uniform grey; panels at high counts closely resemble the target.
figures.caption: Simulation, not a measurement, and not a photograph of skin. All panels share one grey scale. The bottom row is an upper bound no animal can reach - it rewires itself for each target - and it is shown so the compact row can be read against something other than the target.

figures.alt: A short silent animation. The left half holds a fixed one-over-f noise target; the right half shows the modelled skin as the number of independent control channels is stepped up from one to one per actuator, with the channel count and the achieved match score in the panel title. The right half begins as flat grey and progressively resolves into the target texture, with most of the change happening over a single decade of channel count.
figures.caption: Simulation, not a measurement. The same sweep as the fidelity figure, animated over channel count at a fixed motor-unit size of nine. What the animation shows that the curve does not is where the error goes as channels are added: the large-scale blocks resolve first and the fine texture last.
